note: The ONE statement of the glob dialect that routes a repository path to a domain. It had TWO matchers until 2026-08-10 - matchGlob in scripts/memory/store.mjs, which routes a lesson, and a Rust one on the Svod side, which decided which domain skills a member was given - and two matchers over one file agree only by being made to. The Rust matcher is GONE: a member's discretionary skills are now named per seat by the lead (svod/src/lead_skills.rs) instead of derived from the subject, so the routing file has ONE matcher again and scripts/memory/test-store-entries.mjs is its only suite. This file stays, and stays authoritative: the dialect outlived one of its readers and will outlive the next, and the measurement below is why. Measured 2026-08-08, while both existed: the two dialects disagreed on four of the six shapes below, because each side implemented what its author assumed - one a POSIX glob, the other a regex passthrough. Nothing shipped in docs/agent/domain-routing.generated.json used any of the four, so no route was wrong yet; the divergence was waiting for the first skill author to write a class.
dialect: `**` crosses directory separators; `**/` also matches zero components.
`*` matches within one component and never crosses `/`.
`?` is exactly one character and never `/`.
`[abc]` and `[a-z]` are one character from the set, and never `/`.
`[!abc]` and `[^abc]` are one character outside the set, and never `/`.
A `]` in first position is a literal `]`.
An unterminated `[` is a literal `[` rather than swallowing the rest.
dialectAddendum: A pattern and a path are walked as CHARACTERS, not bytes, and one character means one CODE POINT on both sides. The Rust matcher walked UTF-8 bytes until 2026-08-08; the JS regex is built with the `u` flag for the same reason, because without it `[^/]` is one UTF-16 unit and the two disagreed in OPPOSITE directions on an astral character.

A class whose range runs backwards matches nothing, and its negation matches anything but `/`. A JS regex cannot be BUILT from `[z-a]`, so the JS side detects the inversion instead of throwing - a throw would kill lesson routing where the other side merely ignored the rule.
